lambeosaurus:research:1.title: 2026 in archosaur paleontology (research: General non-avian dinosaur research)

facts.statement: The genus Lambeosaurus was named by William A. Parks in 1923.
facts.quote: authority: Parks, 1923

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Lambeosaurus lambei.
facts.quote: type_species: Lambeosaurus lambei

facts.statement: Two other species, L. magnicristatus and L. clavinitialis, were named by Sternberg in 1935.
facts.quote: subdivision: L. magnicristatus Sternberg, 1935 L. clavinitialis? Sternberg, 1935

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period in western North America.
facts.quote: lived during the Late Cretaceous period of western North America

facts.statement: A species named L. laticaudus in 1981 was later reclassified into the separate genus Magnapaulia.
facts.quote: L. laticaudus in 1981 which was later moved to its own genus Magnapaulia

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus is the namesake of the subfamily Lambeosaurinae and the tribe Lambeosaurini.
facts.quote: It is the eponymous member of the subfamily Lambeosaurinae and tribe Lambeosaurini

facts.statement: Adult Lambeosaurus reached lengths of 7 to 7.7 meters and weighed between 2.6 and 3.4 tonnes.
facts.quote: Adult Lambeosaurus would have grown to around 7 - 7.7 m long and weighed 2.6 - 3.4 tonnes

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus was capable of moving on both two legs and four legs.
facts.quote: It was able to move on two or four legs

facts.statement: The dinosaur possessed a highly distinct, hollow cranial crest.
facts.quote: highly distinct, hollow cranial crest

facts.statement: The crest helps identify juvenile Lambeosaurus, which are otherwise nearly indistinguishable from juveniles of Corythosaurus.
facts.quote: The crest also allows for the identification of juveniles, which are otherwise nearly indistinguishable from those of Corythosaurus

facts.statement: The crest developed late in life but expanded in height by an order of magnitude by adulthood.
facts.quote: the crest developing late but expanding in height by an order of magnitude by the time individuals reached adulthood

facts.statement: Skin impressions reveal that Lambeosaurus had unornamented scales covering its entire body.
facts.quote: Skin impressions are known and show that it had unornamented scales across the entire body

facts.statement: Lawrence M. Lambe led three expeditions in 1897, 1898, and 1901 to find fossils in Alberta.
facts.quote: Canadian palaeontologist Lawrence M. Lambe undertook three expeditions in 1897, 1898 and 1901

facts.statement: Lawrence M. Lambe named three new species of Trachodon in 1902.
facts.quote: named Trachodon selwyni, Trachodon marginatus, and Trachodon altidens in 1902

facts.statement: Lawrence M. Lambe concluded that T. marginatus belonged in a new genus he named Stephanosaurus.
facts.quote: Lambe concluded that T. marginatus belonged in a new genus, which he named Stephanosaurus

facts.statement: William A. Parks designated Lambeosaurus lambei for skulls CMN 351 and CMN 2869 in 1923.
facts.quote: designated the new genus and species Lambeosaurus lambei for the complete skulls CMN 351 and CMN 2869 in 1923

facts.statement: Parks chose the name Lambeosaurus lambei to honor Lawrence M. Lambe, who had died in 1919.
facts.quote: Parks chose the name Lambeosaurus lambei to give Lambe, who had died in 1919, as much credit as possible

facts.statement: Charles W. Gilmore described the type material of Lambeosaurus in detail in 1924.
facts.quote: In 1924, American palaeontologist Charles W. Gilmore described the type material of Lambeosaurus in more detail

facts.statement: Gilmore selected skull CMN 2869 as the type specimen for Lambeosaurus lambei.
facts.quote: Gilmore selected the better preserved skull that Lambe described in 1920 (CMN 2869) as the type specimen of Lambeosaurus lambei

facts.statement: A skeleton collected in 1922 was originally identified as Prosaurolophus but was later mounted as a Lambeosaurus being scavenged by Daspletosaurus.
facts.quote: a skeleton missing the skull (FMNH PR 380) collected in 1922 by an expedition of the Field Museum of Natural History, which was originally identified as Prosaurolophus before being prepared and mounted as a Lambeosaurus being scavenged by Daspletosaurus

facts.statement: American Museum of Natural History excavations in the Red Deer River region were conducted primarily by Brown between 1909 and 1914.
facts.quote: The American Museum of Natural History also excavated in the Red Deer River region, primarily through the work of Brown from 1909 to 1914.

facts.statement: American paleontologist William Diller Matthew assigned a small individual discovered by Brown to the genus Procheneosaurus in 1920.
facts.quote: One particularly small individual discovered by Brown, was assigned to as "Procheneosaurus" by American palaeontologist William Diller Matthew in 1920

facts.statement: In 1931, Parks described small crested hadrosaurs found by University of Toronto expeditions in the Red Deer badlands.
facts.quote: In 1931, Parks described more small, crested hadrosaurs found by expeditions of the University of Toronto into the Red Deer badlands.

facts.statement: Specimen ROM 3577 was found around 2 miles southeast of Little Sandhill Creek by L. Sternberg.
facts.quote: The first (ROM 3577) was found around 2 mi southeast of Little Sandhill Creek by L. Sternberg.

facts.statement: Specimen ROM 3578 was found in 1927 by L. Sternberg approximately 1.5 miles downriver of Little Sandhill Creek.
facts.quote: The second specimen, ROM 3578, was found in 1927 by L. Sternberg around 1.5 mi downriver of Little Sandhill Creek.

facts.statement: In 1935, Charles M. Sternberg reassessed crested hadrosaur taxonomy after preparing 18 skulls and skeletons at the Canadian Museum of Nature.
facts.quote: In 1935, Charles M. Sternberg reassessed the taxonomy of crested hadrosaurs after completing the preparation of the 18 skulls and skeletons at the Canadian Museum of Nature.

facts.statement: Charles M. Sternberg found the specimen CMN 8705, used to name Lambeosaurus magnicristatum, in 1919 about 3 miles southwest of the mouth of Little Sandhill Creek.
facts.quote: L. magnicristatum was named for a mostly complete skull and skeleton (CMN 8705) Sternberg found in 1919, about 3 mi southwest of the mouth of Little Sandhill Creek.

facts.statement: Charles M. Sternberg found the specimen CMN 8703, used to name Lambeosaurus clavinitialis, in 1928 approximately 2.5 miles south of the mouth of Berry Creek.
facts.quote: L. clavinitialis was named for a skull and skeleton (CMN 8703) that Sternberg found nearby, also in 1928, ca. 2.5 mi south of the mouth of Berry Creek.

facts.statement: Specimens AMNH 5461 and AMNH 5469 were collected by Brown in Montana in 1916 and assigned to Procheneosaurus erectofrons by Lull and Wright.
facts.quote: Lull and Wright also assigned AMNH 5461 and AMNH 5469 to P. erectofrons, which were collected by Brown in Montana in 1916

facts.statement: William Diller Matthew considered the name Procheneosaurus a nomen nudum (an informal name not valid for taxonomy) in 1921.
facts.quote: Matthew himself did not believe that the description was adequate to name a new taxon, writing to C.M. Sternberg in 1921 that "Procheneosaurus" should be considered a nomen nudum, an informal name not to be used in taxonomy.

facts.statement: The International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature ruled that Tetragonosaurus was not an available name because it lacked a clearly designated type species.
facts.quote: The commission also considered that Tetragonosaurus was not an available name due to lacking a clearly designated type species.

facts.statement: C.M. Sternberg opposed the use of Procheneosaurus in 1953, preferring Tetragonosaurus and believing Procheneosaurus was a nomen nudum.
facts.quote: However, C.M. Sternberg had opposed in 1953 the use of Procheneosaurus over Tetragonosaurus as advocated by Lull and Wright, instead retaining all the species in the latter genus and believing "Procheneosaurus" to be a nomen nudum as suggested by Matthew.

facts.statement: Anatoly K. Rozhdestvensky described the new species Procheneosaurus convincens in 1968, demonstrating links between Asian and North American faunas.
facts.quote: Anatoly K. Rozhdestvensky in 1968, who described the new species Procheneosaurus convincens for an almost complete skeleton and skull from Kazakhstan (PIN 2230), demonstrating links between the Asian and North American faunas.

facts.statement: In 1975, paleontologist Peter Dodson studied how crest shapes change as lambeosaurines grow by comparing fossils to modern reptiles.
facts.quote: In 1975, American palaeontologist Peter Dodson assessed how crest shape changed during growth (ontogeny) in lambeosaurines based on comparisons with modern reptiles and by assuming that smaller individuals were younger.

facts.statement: Peter Dodson analyzed the crests of 36 individuals from 12 named species of Lambeosaurus, Procheneosaurus, and Corythosaurus found in the Oldman Formation.
facts.quote: Dodson reassessed the 12 named species of Lambeosaurus, Procheneosaurus and Corythosaurus believed to have lived together in the Oldman Formation (historic Belly River series), analysing the crests of a total of 36 individuals.

facts.statement: Peter Dodson concluded that smaller Procheneosaurus specimens were juveniles of Lambeosaurus and Corythosaurus, specifically identifying Procheneosaurus praeceps as a juvenile of Lambeosaurus lambei.
facts.quote: He found that the smaller Procheneosaurus specimens were juveniles of the larger Lambeosaurus and Corythosaurus specimens, with Procheneosaurus praeceps being a juvenile form of Lambeosaurus lambei and Procheneosaurus erectofrons and P. cranibrevis being juvenile forms of Corythosaurus.

facts.statement: Peter Dodson proposed that size variation in Lambeosaurus lambei was due to sexual dimorphism, identifying specific museum specimens as males or females.
facts.quote: Dodson also proposed that variation among individuals of the same size was due to sexual dimorphism, resulting in the identifications of ROM 869, CMN 351, YPM 3222 and CMN 8503 as females of L. lambei, and CMN 2869, ROM 1218, ROM 5131, AMNH 5353 and AMNH 5373 as males of L. lambei.

facts.statement: In 1979, John R. Horner assigned jaw bones from Montana's Bearpaw Formation to Lambeosaurus magnicristatus, marking the first lambeosaur found in marine sediments.
facts.quote: In 1979, American palaeontologist John R. Horner assigned partial jaw bones from the Bearpaw Formation of Montana to L. magnicristatus, representing the first lambeosaur specimen from marine sediments.

facts.statement: In 1981, William J. Morris described specimens from Baja California's El Gallo Formation as a tentative new species, Lambeosaurus laticaudus, with type specimen LACM 17715.
facts.quote: In 1981, Morris described specimens excavated from the El Gallo Formation of Baja California between 1968 and 1974 as a new species that he tentatively assigned to Lambeosaurus as ?Lambeosaurus laticaudus, the type specimen of which is LACM 17715.

facts.statement: In a 1990 review, David B. Weishampel and John R. Horner classified Lambeosaurus as including L. lambei, L. magnicristatus, and ?L. laticaudus, while treating other species as synonyms of L. lambei.
facts.quote: In a 1990 review of the Hadrosauridae by American palaeontologists David B. Weishampel and Horner, Lambeosaurus was considered to include L. lambei, L. magnicristatus, and ?L. laticaudus as diagnostic species', while Tetragonosaurus praeceps, L. clavinitialis, and Corythosaurus frontalis were synonyms of L. lambei.

facts.statement: David B. Norman and Hans-Dieter Sues argued that Procheneosaurus convincens was too temporally and spatially distant from Jaxartosaurus to be assigned to any known genus.
facts.quote: British and American palaeontologists David B. Norman and Hans-Dieter Sues, on the other hand, argued that Jaxartosaurus was too separate in time and space from Procheneosaurus convincens, and that although its validity was questionable, it could not be assigned to any known genera.

facts.statement: In 2005, David C. Evans revisited the taxonomy of Tetragonosaurus species with a detailed description of T. erectofrons.
facts.quote: In 2005, Canadian paleontologist David C. Evans revisited the taxonomy of the species of Tetragonosaurus with a more detailed description of T. erectofrons.

facts.statement: David C. Evans and colleagues identified anatomical features that distinguish Corythosaurus from Lambeosaurus regardless of age, aiding juvenile identification.
facts.quote: Evans and colleagues identified features that separated Corythosaurus from Lambeosaurus regardless of age, facilitating the assessments of the juveniles.

facts.statement: In 2007, David C. Evans and Robert R. Reisz redescribed Lambeosaurus magnicristatus.
facts.quote: Evans and Canadian palaeontologist Robert R. Reisz redescribed L. magnicristatus in 2007.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Lambeosaurus magnicristatus (CMN 8705) was largely complete when excavated but suffered significant water damage during storage, requiring the discarding of many limbs and girdles.
facts.quote: The type, CMN 8705, was originally a largely complete skeleton and skull when excavated, but was significantly damaged by water while it was stored and before it could be prepared, and much of the limbs and girdles had to be discarded.

facts.statement: C.M. Sternberg preserved the weathered left side of the L. magnicristatus specimen by reinforcing it with plaster and shipping it in five blocks to Ottawa.
facts.quote: When first discovered, the left side was exposed and had been badly weathered, probably over hundreds of years. To preserve it, Sternberg reinforced the skeleton with plaster and then jacketed it into five separate blocks that were shipped in straw-packed wooden crates to Ottawa.

facts.statement: The 2007 redescription demonstrated that Lambeosaurus magnicristatus can be distinguished from L. lambei based on both anatomy and its geologically younger age.
facts.quote: The 2007 redescription showed that L. magnicristatus can be separated from L. lambei based on its anatomy as well as on its geologically younger age.

facts.statement: While skeletons of L. lambei and L. clavinitialis are completely known, the known skeleton of L. magnicristatus is only 81% complete.
facts.quote: Including all specimens, the skeletons of L. lambei and L. clavinitialis are completely known, and the known skeleton of L. magnicristatus is 81% complete.

facts.statement: A 2022 analysis found L. clavinitialis basal to L. lambei and L. magnicristatus, while a 2014 study noted significant differences in crest morphometrics between L. clavinitialis and the other two species.
facts.quote: A 2022 phylogenetic analysis by Hai Xing and colleagues found L. clavinitialis to be basal to L. lambei and L. magnicristatus, which are sister taxa, and Canadian palaeontologist Kristin S. Brink and colleagues found in 2014 that the crest morphometrics of L. clavinitialis differ significantly from L. lambei and L. magnicristatus.

facts.statement: In 2012, Albert Prieto-Márquez and colleagues redescribed ?L. laticaudus, finding it closest to Velafrons, the only other Mexican lambeosaurine known at the time.
facts.quote: In 2012, Spanish palaeontologist Albert Prieto-Márquez and colleagues redescribed the material of ?L. laticaudus, which was found to be closest to Velafrons, the only other lambeosaurine known from Mexico at the time.

facts.statement: Due to significant anatomical differences from Lambeosaurus species, ?L. laticaudus was reclassified into the new genus Magnapaulia.
facts.quote: It was more distant from the species of Lambeosaurus, and showed enough anatomical differences that they gave it the new genus name Magnapaulia.

facts.statement: In 2013, Kristin S. Brink and Phil R. Bell redescribed Procheneosaurus convincens and established the new genus Kazaklambia due to its distinct features from similar lambeosaurines.
facts.quote: Similarly, the skull of Procheneosaurus convincens was redescribed by Brink and Canadian palaeontologists Phil R. Bell in 2013, who found that it could be differentiated from other lambeosaurines of similar age including Jaxartosaurus, giving if the new genus name Kazaklambia.

facts.statement: Kazaklambia is an early member of Lambeosaurini and is only distantly related to Lambeosaurus.
facts.quote: It has been found to be an early member of Lambeosaurini and only distantly related to Lambeosaurus.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus is distinguished from other hadrosaurids mainly by its skull and crest, while sharing similar anatomy with relatives like Corythosaurus and Hypacrosaurus.
facts.quote: Lambeosaurus is primarily distinguished from other hadrosaurids by its skull and crest, otherwise being very close in anatomy to its close relatives Corythosaurus and Hypacrosaurus.

facts.statement: This large hadrosaurid possessed powerful grinding jaws, a stiffened tail supported by ossified tendons, and elongated limbs indicating it was semi-quadrupedal, a behavior supported by related footprints.
facts.quote: It was a large hadrosaurid, with highly developed jaws full of grinding teeth, a long tail stiffened by ossified tendons that prevented it from drooping, and more elongate limbs suggesting they were semi-quadrupedal (could move on both two legs and all fours), as also shown by footprints of related animals.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus hands had four fingers without a thumb, where the little finger was free and likely used for manipulating objects.
facts.quote: The hands had four fingers, lacking the thumb, and while the second, third, and fourth fingers were bunched together, the little finger was free and could have been used to manipulate objects.

facts.statement: Each foot of Lambeosaurus possessed only the three central toes.
facts.quote: Each foot had only the three central toes.

facts.statement: Species such as L. lambei, L. magnicristatus, and L. clavinitialis grew to approximately 7 to 7.7 meters in length and weighed between 2.6 and 3.4 tonnes.
facts.quote: L. lambei, L. magnicristatus, and L. clavinitialis would have reached around 7 - 7.7 m in length, and 2.6 - 3.4 tonnes in weight.

facts.statement: The skull of Lambeosaurus is distinctively characterized by an elaborate, narrow, and tall crest.
facts.quote: The skull of Lambeosaurus is particularly distinct, bearing an elaborate, narrow and tall crest.

facts.statement: While the crest's form varies between individuals, sexes, and ages, it is consistently oriented perpendicular to the snout.
facts.quote: The form of the crest is variable between individuals, sexes, and ages, but is consistently perpendicular to the snout.

facts.statement: Almost the entire crest is formed by the premaxillae, which elongated and expanded over the skull, rearranging the other skull roof bones.
facts.quote: Almost all of the crest is formed by the premaxillae of the snout, which have elongated and expanded over the skull in a way that has rearranged the other bones of the skull roof.

facts.statement: A rear spur formed by the nasals is present in L. lambei and L. clavinitialis but absent in L. magnicristatus.
facts.quote: A rear "spur" is seen in L. lambei and L. clavinitialis, but absent in L. magnicristatus, which is formed by the nasals.

facts.statement: Inside the crests are S-shaped looping passages connecting the external and internal nostrils, which expand the crest on either side.
facts.quote: Inside the crests there are S-shaped looping passages that connect the external nares (nostrils) with the internal nares, which expand the crest on either side.

facts.statement: An unossified region (fontanelle) exists on the crest sides above the nostril, which shrinks during growth, potentially locking the crest's shape once fully ossified.
facts.quote: On the sides of the crest above the nostril, where the branches of the premaxilla and nasal meet, there is an unossified region (fontanelle) that reduces in size during growth; once fully ossified, the crest might not have been able to change shape further.

facts.statement: The large dentary features a toothless, elongated front region followed by a battery of 40 or 41 vertical columns, each holding up to three functional teeth.
facts.quote: The dentary is large, with an elongate and downturned region at the front that lacked teeth similar to Corythosaurus and Hypacrosaurus, followed by an extensive tooth battery as in the maxilla that contains 40 or 41 vertical columns of up to three functional teeth each.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus teeth are tall relative to their width, have faint edge crenellations, and feature a single strong central keel.
facts.quote: The teeth of both jaws are typical for lambeosaurines, being very tall relative to their width, having very faint crenellations along their edges, and showing a single strong keel along the center.

facts.statement: Only one side of each tooth crown bears enamel for chewing, while the other side is embedded in the jaw bones to form the dental battery columns.
facts.quote: Only one side of the tooth crowns is ornamented and bears enamel for use in chewing (outer side in the maxilla, inner side in the dentary), with the other side embedded in the jaw bones to form columns of functional teeth that compose the dental battery.

facts.statement: The crescentric predentary forms the joint between the dentaries and possesses a sharp cutting edge to support the beak's horn.
facts.quote: The predentary is crescentric, forming the joint between the two dentaries, and with an irregular, sharp, cutting edge to support the horn of a beak.

facts.statement: While the braincase anatomy is consistent with Corythosaurus and Hypacrosaurus, Lambeosaurus uniquely encloses the ophthalmic nerve in a bone tunnel rather than an exposed groove.
facts.quote: The braincase is made up by many fused bones with consistent anatomy between Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, and Hypacrosaurus, though in Lambeosaurus the ophthalmic nerve is enclosed by bone to form a tunnel while in the other genera it is exposed as a groove.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus possessed a neck with 14 or 15 cervical vertebrae, a count intermediate between Olorotitan and Parasaurolophus.
facts.quote: The neck of Lambeosaurus bears 14 or 15 cervical vertebrae, which is fewer than in Olorotitan but more than in Parasaurolophus.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus had 15 to 16 dorsal vertebrae with tall, rectangular spines that were much higher than those of the cervical region.
facts.quote: There were 15 to 16 dorsal vertebrae present in the torso, with the spines much taller than in the cervicals and rectangular.

facts.statement: The scapula of the L. magnicristatus specimen TMP 1966.04.1 was an elongate, flat bone measuring 781 mm in length.
facts.quote: The scapula in the shoulder girdle is an elongate, flat bone, 781 mm long in TMP 1966.04.1 and gently curved as in Corythosaurus.

facts.statement: Although shorter than in Corythosaurus, the humerus remained the most massive bone in the Lambeosaurus arm.
facts.quote: The humerus is relatively shorter than in Corythosaurus, but is still the most massive bone of the arm.

facts.statement: The radius and ulna of Lambeosaurus were longer than the humerus and more robust than those found in Corythosaurus.
facts.quote: The radius and ulna are longer than the humerus as in other lambeosaurines, but are more robust than in Corythosaurus.

facts.statement: The Lambeosaurus femur was massive and columnar, slightly longer than the tibia, consistent with other hadrosaurids.
facts.quote: The femur is massive and columnar, and as in other hadrosaurids it is slightly longer than the tibia of the lower leg.

facts.statement: Measurements from L. clavinitialis show a femur length of 1.02 m, a humerus of 52.0 cm, and an ilium of 1.035 m.
facts.quote: The femur is 1.02 m long in L. clavinitialis, while the humerus is 52.0 cm and the ilium is 1.035 m.

facts.statement: Like other hadrosaurids, the Lambeosaurus foot was reduced to three digits, each ending in a spade-shaped hoof.
facts.quote: The foot in hadrosaurids is reduced to only three digits, which each bear spade-shaped hooves.

facts.statement: Scale impressions have been preserved in three Lambeosaurus specimens: ROM 1218, CMN 8703, and TMP 1966.04.1.
facts.quote: Impressions of scales are known from three specimens of Lambeosaurus, the L. lambei specimen ROM 1218, the L. clavinitialis specimen CMN 8703, and the L. magnicristatus specimen TMP 1966.04.1.

facts.statement: One Lambeosaurus specimen uniquely preserves a 12 mm circular arrangement of eight wedge-shaped feature scales converging to a central point.
facts.quote: Unusually, this specimen also preserves a subcircular 12 mm arrangement of feature scales (larger scales within a matrix of smaller scales) formed by eight wedge-shaped scales converging to one central point.

facts.statement: Extensive skin impressions on L. clavinitialis cover the ribs, the leg before the femur, the hip area, and the first 4 feet of the tail.
facts.quote: The skin impressions of L. clavinitialis are extensive and remain in original position, covering the ribs and leg in front of the femur, the area over the hip, and the first 4 ft of the tail.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus scales were generally small and uniform in size, with the exception of slightly larger scales on the tail.
facts.quote: The scales are relatively small and undifferentiated in size or pattern, though the scales of the tail are slightly larger.

facts.statement: Skin patches on L. magnicristatus along the neck, forelimb, and leg consist of connected raised ridges that may be natural casts of original impressions.
facts.quote: Skin patches on L. magnicristatus were left in original position along the neck, forelimb, and leg, and are unusual in that they consist primarily of connected raised ridges, and thus may represent the natural casts of the original impressions.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus skin patches show a consistent pattern of small, non-overlapping polygonal scales approximately 5 mm in diameter.
facts.quote: The pattern across all patches is consistent, with small polygonal scales around 5 mm in diameter with no overlap or pattern to their arrangement.

facts.statement: Unlike Corythosaurus, Lambeosaurus lacks the enlarged dome-like scales found on the legs of that genus.
facts.quote: In Corythosaurus, enlarged dome-like scales are present on the leg, but these feature scales are absent in Lambeosaurus.

facts.statement: Parks named the genus Lambeosaurus and established the subfamily Lambeosaurinae to replace Stephanosaurinae because no crested skull was known for Stephanosaurus.
facts.quote: Parks named Lambeosaurus and replaced Stephanosaurinae with Lambeosaurinae as no crested skull was now known for Stephanosaurus.

facts.statement: Parks originally limited the subfamily Lambeosaurinae to Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, and Cheneosaurus, though he noted Parasaurolophus shared some similarities.
facts.quote: Parks limited Lambeosaurinae to Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, and Cheneosaurus, but noted that Parasaurolophus showed some similarities as well.

facts.statement: In 1924, Gilmore reclassified Hadrosauridae into three subfamilies, placing Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, Parasaurolophus, Hypacrosaurus, and Cheneosaurus within Lambeosaurinae.
facts.quote: Gilmore revised the classifications of Hadrosauridae in 1924, where he noted that the limited material of Trachodon prevented identifying it as either a crested or non-crested hadrosaur and advocated for abandoning the family named after it, with Hadrosauridae composed of Hadrosaurinae, Saurolophinae, and a Lambeosaurinae that included Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, Parasaurolophus, Hypacrosaurus and Cheneosaurus.

facts.statement: Michael K. Brett-Surman's 1979 phylogeny expanded Lambeosaurinae to include Tsintaosaurus, Jaxartosaurus, and Bactrosaurus, while identifying Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, and Hypacrosaurus as each other's closest relatives.
facts.quote: Following the recognition of cheneosaurs as juveniles of Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, and Hypacrosaurus, American palaeontologist Michael K. Brett-Surman published a phylogeny of all accepted genera of Hadrosauridae in 1979, and expanded Lambeosaurinae to also include Tsintaosaurus, with Jaxartosaurus and Bactrosaurus as early members, and Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus and Hypacrosaurus as one another's closest relatives.

facts.statement: A 1990 review by Weishampel and Horner added Barsboldia and Nipponosaurus to Lambeosaurinae but could not determine if Tsintaosaurus belonged to Lambeosaurinae or Hadrosaurinae.
facts.quote: The 1990 review of hadrosaurs by Weishampel and Horner was unable to conclude if Tsintaosaurus was a lambeosaurine or hadrosaurine, but added the Asian genera Barsboldia and Nipponosaurus to Lambeosaurinae.

facts.statement: In 2011, Robert M. Sullivan and colleagues renamed the group Lambeosaurini because Lambeosaurus, the type genus of Lambeosaurinae, was found to be included within the previously named Corythosaurini.
facts.quote: However, in 2011, American palaeontologist Robert M. Sullivan and colleagues recognized that as Lambeosaurus, the type genus of Lambeosaurinae, was included within Corythosaurini, the group should be more properly called Lambeosaurini.

facts.statement: Polish palaeontologist Daniel Madzia and colleagues named the group Corythosauria in 2021 to unite the subfamilies Parasaurolophini and Lambeosaurini.
facts.quote: The group Corythosauria was then named by Polish palaeontologist Daniel Madzia and colleagues in 2021 to unite the groups Parasaurolophini and Lambeosaurini.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurines are characterized by a single dorsal process at the front of the maxilla that is taller than it is wide, along with an ovoid supratemporal fenestra.
facts.quote: Lambeosaurines are united by the presence of only one process at the front of the maxilla, a dorsal process of the maxilla that is taller than wide, and an ovoid supratemporal fenestra.

facts.statement: Other phylogenetic studies have found Lambeosaurus to be either the most basal lambeosaurine closely related to Corythosaurus, or an intermediate member within Lambeosaurini.
facts.quote: Other results since have found Lambeosaurus as the most basal genus of lambeosaurin, closest to Corythosaurus and deeply nested within Lambeosaurini, or intermediate within Lambeosaurini.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus possessed extensive dental batteries, a unique feeding apparatus also found in ceratopsids.
facts.quote: Lambeosaurus and other hadrosaurs had a unique feeding apparatus of extensive dental batteries, only found elsewhere in ceratopsids, that has been the focus of much research.

facts.statement: Microscopic tooth wear indicates Lambeosaurus used a combination of propalinal and pleurokinetic motions for chewing, involving an oblique up-down stroke and front-back grinding.
facts.quote: The microscopic wear on teeth from chewing shows that it was not purely due to propalinity or kinesis, and instead a combination of both mechanisms contributed to the two-direction chewing motion of hadrosaurs: an oblique up-down power stroke, supplemented by front-back grinding.

facts.statement: Pit marks on Lambeosaurus teeth provide evidence that it consumed fruits and seeds in addition to leaves and stems.
facts.quote: Hadrosaur teeth show more pit marks than ceratopsids, which are known to have had high-fibre diets and also have dental batteries, providing evidence for the consumption of fruits and seeds in Lambeosaurus.

facts.statement: Fewer and smaller microwear scratches on Lambeosaurus teeth suggest it either ate coarser plants or fed higher in the canopy than Prosaurolophus.
facts.quote: Teeth of Lambeosaurus have fewer and smaller microwear scratches than those of Prosaurolophus, which suggests the former had a diet of coarser plants, or fed higher up in the canopy away from the ground.

facts.statement: Lack of microwear scratches and absence of bonebeds suggest Lambeosaurus was a solitary, territorial browser of herbaceous vegetation in closed, forested habitats.
facts.quote: Less scratches may suggest that Lambeosaurus browsed in more closed (forested) habitats than hadrosaurines that fed in open plains, and the additional lack of lambeosaurine bonebeds supports the idea that Lambeosaurus was a closed-habitat browser of herbaceous vegetation that lived solitarily and perhaps with territorial tendencies.

facts.statement: Hypotheses for the crest's function have included underwater feeding, improved smell, thermoregulation, sodium regulation, communication, or sexual identification.
facts.quote: Alternative suggestions have included ideas that the crest served to assist with underwater feeding, an improved sense of smell (olfaction), thermoregulation, sodium regulation, communication, or sexual identification.

facts.statement: In 1962, Ostrom proposed that the crest evolved to redirect the olfactory bulb upwards to increase the sense of smell.
facts.quote: In 1962, Ostrom proposed that the olfactory bulb of the brain, responsible for smell, was redirected upwards into the crest in lambeosaurines to increase the acuity of their sense of smell.

facts.statement: In 1975, Dodson suggested the crest size indicated sexual dimorphism to separate males and females of Lambeosaurus.
facts.quote: Dodson instead suggested in 1975 that the extent of the crest could be used to separate Lambeosaurus into male and female individuals as a form of sexual dimorphism.

facts.statement: Under the resonance hypothesis, juveniles with smaller crests would produce higher-frequency sounds, while adults would produce lower sounds for long-distance socialization.
facts.quote: Under this hypothesis, juveniles with smaller crests would have produced higher-frequency vocalizations, while adults would make lower sounds that would be able to travel across greater distances to assist in socialization.

facts.statement: In 2006, Evans found no evidence of olfactory nerves entering the crest, rejecting the idea that it aided in smell.
facts.quote: In 2006, David Evans conducted the first detailed study of the available braincase material of lambeosaurines. He found that there was no evidence the olfactory nerves entered the nasal loops, and therefore the passages were non-olfactory and the nerves did not branch up into the crest.

facts.statement: Evans suggested acoustic resonance was the primary function of the crest, with visual display as a secondary function.
facts.quote: Evans was thus able to reject Ostrom's idea that the crest aided in a sense of smell, and instead suggested acoustic resonance as the primary driver for its evolution, with visual display as an important secondary function.

facts.statement: In 2009, Evans and colleagues suggested the crest served as a signaling structure for social behavior.
facts.quote: Studies of the brain anatomy of lambeosaurines by Evans and colleagues in 2009 also suggested that the crest served as a signaling structure in social behavior.

facts.statement: During growth, the Lambeosaurus snout became slightly longer while the maxilla, skull height (excluding the crest), and brain size decreased proportionally.
facts.quote: The skull changed in proportions during growth, with the snout becoming slightly longer while the maxilla and height of the skull excluding the crest, as well as the general size of the brain, decreased proportionally.

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus lived in the Dinosaur Park Formation between 76.47 and 74.44 million years ago.
facts.quote: Lambeosaurus is only known from the Dinosaur Park Formation, which has been constrained in age between 76.47 and 74.44 million years ago

facts.statement: The oldest species, Lambeosaurus clavinitialis, lived during the middle Campanian alongside Corythosaurus and Centrosaurus.
facts.quote: L. clavinitialis is the oldest species of Lambeosaurus, found only within the middle Campanian coexisting with Corythosaurus and Centrosaurus

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus lambei lived from the middle to late Campanian, coexisting with Corythosaurus, Centrosaurus, Styracosaurus, and Prosaurolophus.
facts.quote: L. lambei is younger, coexisting with both Corythosaurus and Centrosaurus, as well as Styracosaurus and Prosaurolophus from the middle to late Campanian

facts.statement: Lambeosaurus magnicristatus appeared in the youngest faunal zone around 75.098 million years ago, replacing common megaherbivores.
